fields.Front: In the Java Memory Model, what does the volatile keyword actually guarantee?
fields.Back: Visibility and ordering, not atomicity: a write to a volatile field is immediately visible to all threads and can't be reordered across the access (happens-before edge). It does NOT make compound operations like i++ atomic.

fields.Front: Besides mutual exclusion, what memory-model guarantee does synchronized provide?
fields.Back: Visibility: entering and exiting a synchronized block on the same lock establishes a happens-before relationship, so changes made inside are guaranteed visible to the next thread that acquires that lock.

fields.Front: What is the fundamental compiler-enforced difference between checked and unchecked exceptions in Java?
fields.Back: Checked exceptions (subclasses of Exception but not RuntimeException, e.g. IOException) must be caught or declared with throws or the code won't compile. Unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException/Error subclasses, e.g. NullPointerException) are never enforced by the compiler.

What is the contract between equals() and hashCode() in Java?
fields.Back: If two objects are equal per equals(), they MUST return the same hashCode(). The converse isn't required (unequal objects may share a hash). Violating the forward rule silently breaks hash-based collections like HashMap/HashSet.

fields.Front: How do you correctly override equals() and hashCode() for a class with fields x and y?
fields.Back:
@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (this == o) return true;
    if (!(o instanceof Point p)) return false;
    return x == p.x && y == p.y;
}

@Override
public int hashCode() {
    return Objects.hash(x, y);
}

fields.Front: What does the Java compiler auto-generate for you when you declare a record?
fields.Back: A canonical constructor, private final fields for each component, public accessor methods (named after the components, not getX()), plus equals(), hashCode(), and toString() derived from the component list — the type is implicitly immutable.

What does the bound in <T extends Comparable<T>> mean for a Java generic method?
fields.Back: T must be a type that implements Comparable<T>, so the method body is allowed to call compareTo() on values of type T.

fields.Front: How do you write a generic Java method that returns the larger of two Comparable values?
fields.Back:
public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(T a, T b) {
    return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;
}

fields.Front: Why do generational garbage collectors run frequent young-generation (minor) collections instead of scanning the whole heap each time?
fields.Back: Most objects die young, so a minor GC only has to copy the small fraction of still-live objects out of a small young-gen region — fast and frequent, avoiding the expense of scanning the entire heap on every collection.

fields.Front: When should you prefer ArrayList over LinkedList in Java?
fields.Back: When you need fast random access — get(i) is O(1) on ArrayList (backed by a resizable array) vs O(n) on LinkedList. Prefer LinkedList only for frequent insert/remove at arbitrary positions via an iterator, since ArrayList shifts elements on insert/remove.

What does Spring's @Async annotation do, and how was it used in the Government of Ontario eForm validation microservice?
fields.Back: It runs the annotated method on a separate thread from Spring's task executor, returning control to the caller immediately (often returning a CompletableFuture) instead of blocking. It enabled non-blocking I/O in the high-throughput validation microservice, cutting latency ~40%.

fields.Front: What is the N+1 select problem, and what JPQL fix resolves it (as used at ServiceOntario to cut read latency 40%)?
fields.Back: Lazily fetching N parent entities triggers 1 query for the parents plus N extra queries — one per parent — to load each one's association. Fix: add JOIN FETCH to the JPQL query (e.g. SELECT e FROM Entity e JOIN FETCH e.children) so the association loads in the same query, plus tuning Hibernate's batch-fetch size for remaining lazy loads.

fields.Front: In a Spring Boot service, what does a Resilience4j CircuitBreaker do once a downstream call's failure rate crosses its configured threshold?
fields.Back: It trips to the OPEN state and short-circuits further calls immediately (fast-fail, no wasted latency waiting on a failing dependency) for a wait duration, then moves to HALF_OPEN to test a limited number of calls before deciding whether to close again.

fields.Front: What role does Caffeine caching play in a Spring Boot backend, and what eviction strategies does it support?
fields.Back: It's an in-memory cache (plugged in via Spring's cache abstraction) that avoids repeated expensive calls/DB hits. It supports size-based and time-based eviction (expireAfterWrite/expireAfterAccess) using a near-optimal Window TinyLFU eviction policy.

fields.Front: Java's final keyword applied to a variable
fields.Back: The variable's reference (or primitive value) can be assigned only once; for object references, the referenced object's own internal state can still be mutated unless it's independently immutable.

fields.Text: The JVM divides its runtime data areas into the {{c1::heap}} (shared object storage, garbage collected), the per-thread {{c2::stack}} (local variables and call frames), and the {{c3::method area/metaspace}} (class metadata and static fields).

The core Java Collections Framework interfaces are {{c1::List}} (ordered, duplicates allowed), {{c2::Set}} (no duplicate elements), and {{c3::Map}} (key-value pairs; not itself a subtype of Collection).
